text: Let us start with the problem. Backup jobs fail silently. A cron job stops working, and nobody reads the backup logs until the day they need them.

text: Here is the idea. PostgreSQL writes every change into the write ahead log, the WAL, before it changes a table. Start with a full backup: a copy of the data files.

text: Then archive every piece of WAL to object storage as it is written. In this project that happens at least every sixty seconds.

text: Now you can restore the full copy and replay the WAL up to any second you choose. For example, to four minutes and fifty nine seconds past two, one second before the accident. That is point in time recovery.

text: Two numbers describe how good this is. The RPO, how much data you can lose, is bounded by the sixty second archive interval. And the RTO, how long a restore takes, is something this project measures every single day.

text: The database is PostgreSQL 18. It archives WAL through a dedicated backup host, over mutual TLS. The database itself holds no storage keys and no encryption passphrase.
